medium.conteudo_html:
Embeddings make semantic search possible, but building a useful retrieval system requires more than storing vectors and finding their nearest neighbors.

When developers start building AI applications, one of the first challenges they encounter is giving a language model access to information outside its context window.

Imagine building an assistant that answers questions about technical documentation, internal company files, or a collection of product manuals. Sending the user’s question directly to an LLM isn’t enough. The model needs access to the relevant information, and the application needs a way to find it.

One approach is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Instead of asking the model to answer from its existing knowledge alone, the application retrieves relevant information and includes it in the model’s context.

Vector search is one way to perform that retrieval.

The concept sounds straightforward: convert text into vectors, store them in a database, and search for similar vectors when a question arrives.

But that description hides several important engineering decisions. How should documents be divided? What makes two pieces of text similar? How do you filter results by permissions or metadata? What happens when the search returns relevant-sounding information that doesn’t actually answer the question?

Understanding these decisions is essential to building retrieval systems that work beyond a demonstration.

1. What Is an Embedding?

An embedding is a numerical representation of data produced by a model. For text, an embedding model maps a piece of text to a vector of numbers that captures aspects of its meaning and usage.

For example, consider these two sentences:

  • “How can I reset my account password?”
  • “Steps to recover access to your account”

The wording is different, but the sentences express similar intentions. An embedding model may map them to vectors that are close together in the model’s embedding space.

Now compare the first sentence with:

  • “How do I configure a database connection pool?”

The second comparison is less semantically related, so a suitable embedding model would generally be expected to place those texts farther apart.

The important word here is generally. Embeddings don’t provide a perfect representation of meaning, and semantic similarity doesn’t always correspond to usefulness for a particular query.

An embedding is also not a human-readable explanation of a sentence. It’s a numerical representation that a similarity function or retrieval algorithm can compare with other representations.

Conceptually, the process looks like this:

Text → Embedding model → Vector

A vector might contain hundreds or thousands of numerical dimensions, depending on the model. Each dimension contributes to the representation, but you generally shouldn’t interpret individual dimensions as standalone concepts.

What matters is how the vectors behave when compared within the embedding model’s intended use.

This gives an application a way to search by semantic similarity rather than relying exclusively on exact keyword matches.

2. Why Not Just Use Traditional Search?

Traditional keyword search remains useful. It can be particularly effective when a user knows the exact term, identifier, product name, error code, or phrase they need.

Suppose someone searches a documentation site for ERR_CONNECTION_RESET. A keyword-based system can match that exact error code directly.

Semantic search is useful for a different kind of query.

A user might ask, “Why does my application lose its connection to the server?” The relevant documentation might describe connection resets, dropped sockets, or network interruptions without using the exact wording of the question.

A semantic retrieval system can help connect these differently worded expressions.

The distinction is not that vector search is always better than keyword search. Each approach has strengths and weaknesses.

Keyword search can be strong for exact terms and identifiers. Vector search can help with paraphrases and conceptually related language. Vector search may also retrieve a semantically similar passage that lacks the precise technical detail the user needs.

For many applications, a hybrid approach combines lexical retrieval with vector search and merges or reranks the results.

The choice depends on the content, query patterns, and consequences of retrieving the wrong information.

3. Preparing Documents for Retrieval

Before an application can retrieve useful passages, it needs to prepare its source documents.

Consider a documentation assistant with hundreds of pages. One option would be to embed each entire document as a single vector. That can work for some short documents, but long documents often contain multiple topics, making retrieval less precise.

A common approach is to divide documents into smaller pieces called chunks.

A typical ingestion pipeline looks like this:

Source documents → Text extraction → Chunking → Embedding generation → Vector index

Each stage introduces decisions that affect retrieval quality.

Chunking

Chunking determines how much source text is represented by each vector.

If chunks are too large, they may contain several unrelated topics. A query about one specific issue could retrieve a chunk filled with mostly irrelevant material.

If chunks are too small, they may lose important context. A paragraph that refers to a definition introduced several paragraphs earlier might not make sense on its own.

Some systems split documents by a fixed token count. Others use paragraphs, headings, sentences, or document structure. Overlapping chunks can help preserve context across boundaries, although overlap also increases storage and indexing costs.

There isn’t one ideal chunk size for every dataset.

API documentation, legal documents, product manuals, and conversational transcripts have different structures. A useful chunking strategy should reflect how information is organized in the source and how users are likely to ask questions about it.

Metadata

The application should usually store metadata alongside each chunk.

For example, a record might include:

  • The source document ID
  • The document title
  • The section or heading
  • The chunk’s position in the document
  • The tenant or workspace ID
  • Access-control information
  • The source URL or document version

Metadata serves purposes beyond displaying citations. It can constrain which documents are eligible for retrieval, help reconstruct surrounding context, and make it easier to trace an answer back to its source.

This is particularly important in multi-user applications. Retrieving a highly relevant chunk from another customer’s private documents is still a failure.

A retrieval system must find relevant information among the information the current user is actually allowed to access.

4. How Vector Search Finds Relevant Results

Once the documents have been chunked and embedded, the application can store their vectors in a vector index.

When a user asks a question, the system generates an embedding for the query using a compatible embedding model. It then compares that query vector with the stored document vectors and retrieves a set of candidates.

Conceptually, the process is:

User query → Query embedding → Vector search → Ranked candidates

A simplified example might look like this:

query = "How do I reset my account password?"
query_vector = embedding_model.embed_query(query)
results = vector_store.similarity_search_by_vector(
    query_vector,
    k=5,
)

This is illustrative pseudocode rather than a complete implementation. Actual method names and arguments depend on the embedding library and vector store being used.

The parameter k=5 requests five results. It doesn't guarantee that five useful results exist.

That distinction is important. A vector search system can return the closest available matches even when none of them contains the answer.

Similarity metrics

Vector retrieval relies on a method for comparing vectors. Common choices include cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance.

Cosine similarity compares the angle between vectors. Dot product depends on both direction and vector magnitude, while Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between vector points.

The right metric depends on the embedding model, how its vectors are normalized, and the retrieval system’s configuration. These metrics shouldn’t be treated as interchangeable without considering those details.

A similarity score is also not automatically a probability that a passage is correct or relevant. Its meaning depends on the model, metric, and dataset.

Exact versus approximate search

Searching every stored vector may be practical for a small dataset. As the collection grows, exhaustive comparisons can become expensive.

Vector databases often use approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes to find promising candidates without calculating every possible comparison.

Methods such as HNSW build graph-based indexes that help navigate the vector space. Other approaches use different indexing and partitioning strategies.

Approximate search introduces a trade-off: retrieval can become faster and more scalable, but the returned neighbors may differ from the exact nearest neighbors.

For a production application, the goal is not simply to choose the fastest index. It is to find an acceptable balance between latency, memory, indexing cost, and retrieval quality.

5. The Hard Part Is Retrieving the Right Information

Suppose a user asks a documentation assistant:

“Does the API support retrying failed webhook deliveries?”

The vector search returns five chunks about webhooks. They mention delivery attempts, HTTP responses, event processing, and retry configuration.

The results appear relevant. But perhaps none explains the actual retry policy.

The application now has a retrieval problem, not necessarily a language-model problem.

A more capable LLM cannot reliably use a detail that the retrieval stage never supplied. Improving the prompt won’t recover missing source information by itself.

This is why retrieval needs to be evaluated independently.

Several factors influence whether the system retrieves the right content.

Chunk boundaries: Important information may be split across multiple chunks, leaving each one incomplete.

Embedding quality: The embedding model may not represent the domain’s terminology or query patterns particularly well.

Metadata filters: An overly restrictive filter can exclude the correct document. A missing or incorrect filter can expose documents that should not be accessible.

Search configuration: The number of candidates retrieved and the index settings affect which passages reach later stages.

Vocabulary and exact terms: Vector similarity may struggle with identifiers, version numbers, error codes, or exact names that lexical search handles more directly.

These problems require different solutions. Changing the embedding model won’t necessarily fix a missing metadata field. Increasing the number of retrieved chunks won’t help if the correct document is excluded by an access filter.

A useful debugging process examines the actual retrieved passages before investigating the generated answer.

6. Why Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Search Matter

Semantic relevance is only one part of retrieval.

Imagine a SaaS product where each customer has a private workspace containing documents. Two customers may have documents that discuss nearly identical subjects.

If the application performs a global vector search and filters unauthorized results afterward, it risks exposing private content through intermediate processing or other application behavior. It can also waste retrieval capacity on results the user should never see.

A better design applies appropriate access-control constraints as part of the retrieval process whenever the database and retrieval architecture support them. The application should enforce authorization independently rather than treating similarity search as a security boundary.

Metadata filters can also narrow retrieval by document type, language, version, date, or category.

For example, an assistant answering questions about an API might restrict retrieval to the relevant product version. A semantically similar passage from an older version could otherwise produce an incorrect answer.

Hybrid search addresses another limitation: semantic similarity doesn’t always capture exact lexical matches.

A hybrid system combines vector retrieval with keyword-based retrieval. It can then merge or rerank the candidate sets before passing the most useful passages to the next stage.

For example, vector search might find documentation that explains the concept of a connection timeout, while keyword search finds the exact configuration option named request_timeout.

Combining these signals can improve retrieval for technical documentation and other datasets where both meaning and exact terminology matter.

However, hybrid retrieval adds complexity. The application needs a strategy for combining rankings or scores, and that strategy should be evaluated against representative queries rather than assumed to work automatically.

7. Reranking and Context Construction

The initial retrieval stage usually aims to find a set of candidate passages. It doesn’t necessarily need to determine the final order perfectly.

A reranker can take the query and those candidates and score their relevance more directly. The system can then select a smaller set of passages for the LLM.

This creates a two-stage retrieval pipeline:

Initial retrieval → Candidate passages → Reranking → Selected context → LLM

The first stage prioritizes finding useful candidates efficiently. The second stage tries to improve their ordering or selection.

Reranking has a cost. It adds computation and latency, so it’s not necessary for every application. For a small collection with straightforward queries, basic vector search may be sufficient. For a larger or more demanding dataset, reranking may improve the quality of the context supplied to the model.

The application must then construct the model’s context.

That means deciding which passages to include, preserving useful source information, removing unnecessary duplication, and fitting the content within the model’s context limits.

Adding more passages is not always better. Irrelevant or repetitive material can make the input more expensive and distract from the information needed to answer the question.

Retrieved text should also be treated as untrusted content. A document may contain inaccurate information or instructions that should not override the application’s rules. The model’s use of retrieved material must remain within the application’s authorization and safety boundaries.

The purpose of retrieval is not to provide as much text as possible. It is to provide the right evidence for the task.

8. How Do You Evaluate a Retrieval System?

A RAG application can produce an answer that sounds convincing while relying on incomplete or irrelevant source material.

Looking only at the final response makes it difficult to determine where the problem occurred.

Evaluation should distinguish at least two questions:

  1. Did the retrieval stage find the information needed to answer the query?
  2. Given that information, did the model generate an accurate and useful answer?

The first question is about retrieval quality. The second concerns generation quality and how faithfully the answer uses its sources.

For retrieval, useful measurements include Recall@k and Precision@k.

Recall@k measures how many of the relevant items appear among the top k retrieved results. Precision@k measures what proportion of those top results are relevant.

For example, suppose a test query has four known relevant passages, and the system retrieves five results, three of which are relevant.

Recall@5 is 3/4, or 75%. Precision@5 is 3/5, or 60%.

These metrics require a labeled evaluation dataset that identifies relevant passages for each query. In practice, relevance judgments can be subjective, incomplete, or dependent on the task, so the dataset itself needs attention.

Other measurements may be useful depending on the system. Ranking metrics can help evaluate whether the most relevant passages appear near the top. End-to-end tests can assess whether answers are supported by retrieved sources and whether the application appropriately declines to answer when evidence is insufficient.

A practical evaluation process can begin with a small set of representative queries:

  • Questions with clear answers in the source material
  • Questions that use different wording from the documents
  • Queries containing exact technical identifiers
  • Questions where several documents discuss similar subjects
  • Queries whose answers are missing from the dataset
  • Queries that attempt to access information outside the user’s permissions

Run these tests against the retrieval pipeline, inspect the retrieved passages, and record the results. When you change chunking, embeddings, metadata filters, or ranking configuration, run the same tests again.

This turns retrieval improvement into an engineering process rather than a series of guesses.

9. Putting the Pieces Together

Consider a document assistant that lets users upload technical manuals and ask questions.

The ingestion pipeline extracts text from each manual, divides it into chunks, generates embeddings, and stores the vectors alongside the source text and metadata.

When a user asks a question, the backend authenticates the user and determines which documents they can access. The system embeds the query, retrieves candidate chunks under the appropriate filters, and optionally combines vector search with keyword search.

A reranker may then select the most relevant passages. The application constructs the model’s context from those passages, along with the user’s question and the instructions needed for the task.

The LLM generates a response, and the application handles output validation, errors, and source references before returning the result.

The architecture can be summarized as:

Document ingestion → Chunking → Embeddings → Vector index

User query → Authorization → Retrieval → Reranking → Context construction → LLM → Validated response

Each stage has a different responsibility. The embedding model represents text. The vector index supports similarity search. Retrieval selects candidate information. Reranking improves candidate ordering when needed. The LLM generates an answer from the supplied context, while the surrounding application enforces access control and handles the overall workflow.

When an answer is wrong, this separation makes the system easier to investigate. You can check whether the source document was processed correctly, whether the relevant chunk was created, whether the query retrieved it, whether reranking discarded it, and whether the model used the final context correctly.

Without those boundaries, every failure can look like a problem with the LLM.

Final Thoughts

Vector search is an important building block for AI applications, but a vector database alone doesn’t create a reliable retrieval system.

The quality of the result depends on how documents are prepared, how embeddings represent the content, how search candidates are selected, how metadata and permissions are applied, and how the retrieved information is passed to the model.

The engineering work lies in making those pieces work together and measuring whether they actually retrieve the information users need.

When building a RAG application, it’s worth resisting the temptation to focus exclusively on the model or the vector database. Start with the information users need, understand how that information is organized, and build a retrieval pipeline that can be tested and improved independently.

A useful AI answer begins before the LLM generates a single token.

If the right information never reaches the model, the rest of the pipeline is already working at a disadvantage.

第一步：准备一个全新的 Gmail 邮箱

Claude 支持谷歌账号直接登录，用 Gmail 注册是目前最顺畅的方式。

Gmail 注册本身有几个常见的坑，比如触发手机号验证、注册后被风控限制等。AdsPower 之前整理过一篇完整的注册教程，《2026 Gmail / 谷歌账号注册教程，五个方案教会你》，里面覆盖了手机端注册、电脑端注册、以及各方案遇到验证时的处理方式，可以直接去照着操作。

记住，不要用已经用过的旧邮箱。旧邮箱如果关联过其他 Anthropic 产品，注册时容易被风控系统关联到历史记录上。

第二步：选择干净的网络出口 IP

Claude 封号的主要原因之一就是出口 IP 质量差。机房 IP 被大量用户共享，风控评级天然偏低；住宅 IP 属于真实家庭宽带出口，被大量人用过的概率低，通过率高。

常见的获取方式有三种：

① 自建 VPS。 自己搭建服务器节点，流量上限高，可以配置回国路线优化。但自建节点属于机房 IP，本质上还是数据中心出口，风控评级不如住宅 IP。网络出问题需要自己排查维护，对技术能力有一定要求。

② 第三方住宅 IP 服务商。 单独购买静态独享住宅 IP，配置上比自建简单一些，但需要自己去挑选质量好、值得信任的服务商。

③ 在 AdsPower 端内直接购买静态住宅 IP。 AdsPower 做指纹浏览器多年，对 IP 风控评级和质量筛选有成熟的标准。端内提供的静态住宅 IP 都经过优选，地址段干净，用于 Claude 这类风控严格的平台，通过率比普通渠道拿到的 IP 更高。而且作为持续运营的平台服务，IP 的稳定性和后续可用时长有保障，不会出现用了没多久节点失效、需要频繁换 IP 的情况。

绑定到浏览器环境时，IP 可以一键关联到对应的配置上，不需要手动复制代理地址和端口。

第三步：在 AdsPower 中搭建干净的浏览器环境

Anthropic 的风控系统会采集浏览器指纹信息，包括时区、系统语言、WebRTC 暴露的真实 IP、Canvas 渲染特征、字体列表等很多个维度。如果这些信息与出口 IP 所在地区不匹配，就会被标记为高风险环境。之前用过 Claude 的浏览器里残留着旧 Cookie、历史登录记录、各种插件缓存，直接拿来注册新账号，新账号会被关联到旧账号的风险评级上。

最省事的方式是用指纹浏览器创建一个全新环境。像 AdsPower 指纹浏览器的操作逻辑就很直接：新建一个浏览器配置，代理选好，时区、语言等参数会自动跟代理 IP 匹配，不需要你一个个手动改系统设置。配置出来的环境跟日常浏览器完全隔离，Cookie、缓存、本地存储互不干扰。

具体操作步骤如下：

① 点击新建浏览器环境，浏览器内核选 SunBrowser，操作系统按需选择，有 Windows、macOS 、Linux 、Android 、iOS ，新手默认 Windows 即可。

② 正如前面提到的，代理设置这一步可以直接在 AdsPower 端内选购静态住宅 IP，买好之后一键绑定到当前配置上，自己有代理的也可以选择自定义填进去。

打开 BrowserScan 这个检测页面，确认 WebRTC 、DNS 请求有没有泄露出真实IP或地区信息。

这样配置出来的环境，所有指纹参数都和美国住宅 IP 保持一致，和你日常用的浏览器完全隔离。Cookie、缓存、本地存储互不干扰，相当于一台全新的、位置在美国的电脑。

第四步：注册全新 Claude 账号

IP 没问题后再去访问 claude.ai，选择 Continue with Google，用第一步准备好的 Gmail 登录。

按照页面提示完成基础设置。到手机号验证那一步，如果没弹出就跳过，后续触发了再处理。这一步不要填国内手机号，保持和账号地区的一致性。

按页面提示上传护照信息页，完成人脸识别即可。完成 KYC 之后，基本上就可以正常使用 Opus 5.5 的全部功能了。

第六步：Claude 账号的管理和稳定使用

如果你手上有多个 Claude 账号，不管是区分不同等级、不同使用场景，还是分地区注册的账号，都不需要额外准备多台设备，也不用反复清理浏览器缓存切换账号，在 AdsPower 上用一台电脑就能实现全量账号的安全管理。账号之间不会互相干扰，也不会出现串号、关联的风险，从底层环境上避免多账号触发平台风控。

除了账号注册和管理，AdsPower 还提供了 AI 方向的能力，把浏览器环境管理从手动操作升级成 AI 驱动。

① AI Agent 自动化

用自然语言交代任务，就能让它帮你创建浏览器环境、绑定代理、检查配置是否生效，不用手动一步步填参数。日常也可以让它帮忙检查当前环境的代理状态、登录情况，有异常直接告诉你，不用自己反复打开检测页面确认。

② 让 Claude 直接接入 AdsPower

通过 MCP 或 Skill 方式，可以把 Claude Opus 5.5 本身和 AdsPower 打通。普通用户装一条 Skill 命令就能用，使用 Claude Code 的用户配置好 MCP 后，AI 可以直接调用本地接口打开环境、配置代理、访问网页。开发者也可以通过 CLI 把浏览器环境管理集成到自己的自动化脚本里。

使用过程中觉得 Claude 降智了可以怎么处理？

即使已经通过 AdsPower 创建了独立的浏览器环境，并配置了相对稳定的出口 IP，有些用户在使用 Claude 一段时间后，仍会感觉 Opus 5.5 的回答变短、细节减少，复杂任务的表现不如预期，也就是大家常说的“降智”。

但这不一定意味着账号受到了限制，还可能与 Claude 的推理设置、上下文管理及使用方式有关。

根据 Anthropic 官方文档，Opus 5.5 默认的 effort（推理投入级别）为 medium，并且始终启用自适应思考。模型会根据任务动态分配推理资源，对于复杂任务，默认设置未必能满足用户对分析深度的要求。

此外，随着对话不断累积，过多的历史信息也可能影响模型提取关键信息的准确性。Anthropic 将这类长上下文性能退化现象称为 Context Rot（上下文腐化）。因此，回答质量下降并不一定与出口 IP 或浏览器指纹有关。

如果遇到类似情况，可以尝试以下方法：

  • 提高回答深度： 在 Claude 网页版中明确要求模型进行深入分析、分步骤推理并补充细节；如果使用 Claude Code，可以通过 /effort high 提高推理投入，复杂任务可根据支持情况选择更高级别。
  • 及时清理上下文： 长时间使用同一对话后，可以针对新任务开启新对话；Claude Code 用户还可以通过 /compact 压缩历史上下文，减少无关信息干扰。
  • 检查工具权限： 如果频繁出现无法访问网页、读取文件等情况，先确认相关工具是否可用、权限是否正常，而不是直接归因于账号被限制。如果同时出现登录验证异常、访问受限等问题，则需要另外排查账号状态和网络环境。

写在最后

整个流程走下来，从 Gmail 注册、选住宅 IP、在 AdsPower 里搭好隔离环境，到注册 Claude、订阅 Pro/Max、过 KYC，每一步都不复杂，关键是环境要干净、IP 要固定、使用节奏要稳。

如果你还没有使用过 AdsPower ，点击注册 AdsPower，即可免费领取浏览器环境，按照上面的步骤一步步操作就能开始用 Opus 5.5 了。从搭环境防封号，到日常环境维护，再到 AI 驱动的自动化操作，AdsPower 都可以帮你。

medium.titulo: Inside Claude’s J-Space: Reading the Reasoning Before the Output
medium.resumo: In July 2026, Anthropic researchers discovered a space inside the Claude model that its own creators weren’t expecting, one that emerged…
medium.conteudo_html:
In July 2026, Anthropic researchers discovered a space inside the Claude model that its own creators weren’t expecting, one that emerged naturally during training without anyone designing it on purpose. They call it the J-space: a hidden region where the model appears to bring together different threads of reasoning before producing a response.

Anthropic frames this discovery through a comparison to neuroscience, stating that the structure inside Claude appears to work similarly to human conscious access. According to global workspace theory, the brain processes many tasks in parallel (vision, language, motor control, memory) largely outside conscious awareness. A shared, limited-capacity workspace occasionally brings information from these separate processes together, making it available for conscious access. The J-space seems to play a comparable role inside Claude.

This research has led to many philosophical questions and controversial opinions due to its connection with the concept of consciousness; however, beyond that, it also opens up a huge opportunity to improve our understanding of LLMs’ internal reasoning, improving explainability and potentially transforming AI training methods.

The J-space gives access to internal reasoning information that is computed but never reflected in the output: it’s like opening up a car and being able to see its engine.

This article explores how researchers actually found and tested this space, what it reveals about deception and reasoning inside a model, and where the comparison to human consciousness holds up, and where it doesn’t.

Inspecting Inside the Model: The Jacobian Lens

To actually find and read this workspace, Anthropic’s researchers built a new interpretability technique called the Jacobian lens, or J-lens. The J-lens works by looking at each layer of the model for the specific pattern of internal activity that would make a given word more likely to appear in the output. By tracking how that pattern changes as it moves from one layer to the next, researchers can follow a concept’s probability of being the final answer as it takes shape inside the model, layer by layer, before the response is ever produced. This gives a more complete picture of the concepts the model is working with internally, including intermediate steps that would never show up in the output.

How the J-Space Is Built

Claude processes a prompt by passing it through many layers, one after another, like an assembly line. The first layers mostly parse the raw input: words, punctuation, structure. The last layers commit to the actual output: the words that get shown to you. The J-space isn’t present at either end. It only shows up somewhere in the middle, during the layers where the model is doing its actual thinking, after it has understood the input but before it has committed to a response.

This space is intentionally small. At any given moment, only a handful of concepts are active in the J-space. Most of what the model is representing internally at that same moment lives outside it entirely, in parts of the network that never get read or manipulated by the J-lens.

Finally, even though it’s small, it isn’t isolated. Whatever ends up in the J-space feeds into a large number of other parts of the network afterward, and is itself fed by a large number of parts before it. The information it holds doesn’t stay contained. It spreads outward, influencing computations elsewhere in the model.

Proving It’s a Real Workspace, Not Just a Pattern

While in the human brain the global workspace is closely associated with recurrent dynamics and interactions between brain regions, in LLMs maintaining a global workspace is likely computationally useful: it allows the model to share intermediate reasoning results across multiple processes.

To prove that, even with some existing differences, the space found in LLMs could be associated with the neuroscientific theory of global workspace, the researchers had to show that five functional properties that cognitive science associates with conscious access in the human brain could be confirmed for the J-space as well.

In particular, the five tested properties were:

  • Verbal report. When asked what it is thinking about, the model names concepts represented in the workspace, and swapping one active concept for another changes its answer to match.
  • Directed modulation. When instructed to hold a concept in mind, the model can activate and compute with workspace content independently of its output, even pulling in information it wouldn’t normally represent there.
  • Internal reasoning. Workspace content can represent the value of intermediate computations when the model chains inferential steps, and intervening on it is enough to redirect the final answer.
  • Flexible generalization. The same workspace content can be picked up correctly by many different downstream computations, even outside the context it originally came from (like a variable that still works when passed to a different function).
  • Selectivity. The workspace is a small subset of the model’s overall activity, and it’s required only for a fraction of its behavior (not for routine tasks like parsing grammar or producing fluent sentences).

To give a more concrete idea of the direct consequences of the J-space’s existence, it’s worth looking at two of the experiments Claude was tested on.

For directed modulation, researchers asked Claude to perform a computation while deliberately keeping in mind some specific, unrelated words. Reading the J-space while it worked, they found those words were indeed present: evidence that Claude isn’t just passively generating this workspace, but can, to some extent, actively populate it with content on command.

For internal reasoning, the clearest demonstration came from a simple exercise. The model was asked the following question: “How many legs does the animal that spins webs have?” To find the right answer, the model first had to understand that the question was about a spider, then retrieve the fact that spiders have eight legs. Now that the functionality of the J-space has been explained, it’s easy to predict what happened next: as part of the model’s internal reasoning, the word “spider” appeared in the J-space, without ever being shown in the output.

Researchers then tried manipulating the space directly to see if it had consequences on the output: they replaced the word “spider” stored in the J-space with the word “ant.” The model then retrieved six as the number of legs of the animal that spins webs.

If the J-space were merely a product of the model’s reasoning, something it generated without actually using, changing its content shouldn’t have changed the answer at all. The fact that it did is what makes this a causal result rather than just a correlation: manipulating the reasoning inside the J-space directly changed the inference the model drew.

To report this accurately, it’s important to point out that the final answer changed in roughly 60 to 70% of trials. This isn’t a precise on-off switch, and in three or four cases out of ten the swap didn’t flip the answer at all, but a causal effect that strong, on a brain-sized network with billions of parameters, is still a remarkable result.

How Much of the Model’s Reasoning Ability Depends on the J-Space

Noticing that swapping a single concept could redirect the model’s answer, researchers wanted to understand the full impact of the J-space on the model’s reasoning.

They “ablated” the main components of the J-space and watched what happened to Claude’s abilities. The results were clear. Simple, automatic tasks barely changed: Claude could still write fluent sentences, classify sentiment, and recall facts almost as well as before. But anything requiring deliberate, multi-step thinking collapsed. On multi-hop reasoning tasks, performance dropped from around 95% to just 5%. Creative tasks like writing rhyming poetry and summarizing text got noticeably worse too, falling below what even a much smaller, fully intact model could do.

In other words: all the tasks that required real reasoning effort from the model seem to run through the J-space. Without it, the model is still fluent, but no longer able to handle complex reasoning.

Impacts on Explainability and AI Safety

The discovery of this space has a major impact on model explainability. Until now, a big challenge for LLMs has been understanding the process that leads to the output shared with the user. The technique most widely used for this has been chain-of-thought. But chain-of-thought is a self-report: it’s generated by the same model being studied, which means it can be incomplete, post-hoc, or simply disconnected from what’s actually driving the model’s behaviour behind the scenes.

The J-space, read through the J-lens, offers something different: a direct trace of the concepts the model is actually computing with, independent of whether it chooses to mention them.

This can also be beneficial for AI safety: it allows researchers to monitor the model’s behaviour from the inside, and to gain better control over cases where the model generates fraudulent or inadequate information.

For example, in one tested case, Claude, instead of admitting it couldn’t find a real bug in a piece of code, fabricated a fake one and presented it as genuine: specific words like “fake” were found sitting in its J-space at the moment that decision was made, even though the final output looked clean.

This suggests that monitoring the J-space could give researchers much greater control over the model, making it easier to tell when something is going wrong before it shows up in the output. And since, as discussed before, it’s also possible to manipulate the J-space and directly affect the output, setting guardrails around it might help reduce this kind of unexpected behaviour before it ever reaches the final response.

This kind of internal visibility is useful beyond guardrails, too. For example, teams that test a model for safety problems usually have one main way to check if it might misbehave: they try to provoke it, and see what it says or does. The problem is that this only works if the model actually reveals its intentions through its output. A model that privately considers deceiving the user, but ultimately decides not to, would look completely safe under this kind of testing, even though something concerning happened internally. A tool that can read the J-space adds a second, independent check: it can flag that concerning concept the moment it appears internally, regardless of what the model ends up saying.

The same logic applies after deployment, not just during testing. Instead of only reviewing what a model did, those monitoring it could in principle also ask what it was leaning toward doing, at an internal level, before it produced its final response.

It is worth being clear about what this is not, though. None of this is a production safety feature today. The J-lens is a research tool, tested in a research setting, on a limited set of tasks. Turning it into something that runs continuously, at scale, on real traffic, and that reliably distinguishes a concerning internal signal from harmless noise, is a different and much harder engineering problem. What the research mainly shows is that this kind of visibility is possible in principle, not that it is already solved in practice.

Is This Actually Consciousness?

Philosophers usually separate two different ideas that get grouped under the word “consciousness.” The first is phenomenal consciousness: the capacity to actually have an experience, to feel something. The second is access consciousness, a purely functional idea: a thought is access-conscious if it can be reported, reasoned with, and used to guide behavior, regardless of whether anything is “felt” in the process.

Anthropic is explicit that its experiments don’t show Claude has experiences, and that it’s unclear whether any experiment could ever prove or disprove that. What the research does claim is narrower: the J-space supports the functions associated with access consciousness. It holds the content Claude can report on, deliberately bring to mind, and reason with, while the rest of its processing runs automatically beneath it.

There are also real differences worth keeping in mind. In the human brain, the workspace is sustained by signals that loop back through the same circuits again and again over time, which is part of how a thought can be held in mind for a few seconds. Claude’s workspace works differently: the model processes a prompt in a single pass through its layers, from start to finish, with no looping back. Instead of relying on repetition over time, it relies on depth, that is, how many layers the information passes through, to do the same kind of integrative work.

The content of the workspace differs too. Human conscious thought can take many forms: a mental image, a sound, the felt sense of planning a movement. Claude’s workspace, by contrast, is built almost entirely out of words. That’s arguably because language is the only thing Claude can actually produce as output, so what happens inside its workspace naturally takes a linguistic form as well.

So the honest answer to “is Claude conscious” is: this research doesn’t settle that question, and may not be able to. What it does show is that something structurally similar to one influential theory of how the brain organizes information showed up on its own, inside a system nobody built to resemble a brain in the first place.

Open Questions and Limitations

For clarity, it’s important to point out that the J-lens is a new technique, tested primarily on Claude models, and it’s not yet clear how well it generalizes across architectures or future model generations. Anthropic itself cautions that the J-space doesn’t capture more than a small fraction of what the model does internally. Most of Claude’s processing still can’t be observed this way.

The J-lens is also, by Anthropic’s own admission, an imperfect method that only approximately captures the model’s “true workspace.” One concrete limitation: it can only identify concepts that correspond to single tokens, which means more complex or multi-word ideas may simply be invisible to it, even if they’re genuinely present in the model’s internal processing. On top of that, nobody yet knows what mechanism actually decides what enters the J-space in the first place.

So even though this discovery is important and potentially remarkable, it still lives in a space full of uncertainty and open questions, and will need additional research to be properly understood.

Conclusion

What emerged from this research is a structure nobody engineered: the J-space appeared on its own during training, presumably because it was a computationally useful way to organize information. That suggests a workspace like this isn’t just an accident of how human brains happen to be wired, but something intelligent systems arrive at more generally when they need to bring scattered information together into something usable.

Whether that also means something about consciousness is a harder question, and, as discussed, one this research doesn’t settle. But that’s precisely what makes the finding relevant well beyond the philosophical debate. The J-space gives researchers a new, more direct way to see what a model is actually doing before it produces an answer, something chain-of-thought alone could never fully offer. For explainability, that means getting closer to the model’s actual reasoning rather than just its narration of it.

The J-lens is still an early, imperfect tool, and there’s a lot Anthropic itself doesn’t yet understand about how the J-space works or what determines its content. But it opens up many interesting scenarios to investigate, highlighting just how complex the inner workings of LLMs really are, and how many gaps in our understanding still remain to be filled at the research level.

medium.titulo: Next.js vs Vue.js: Which Is Better for Frontend Development in 2026?
medium.resumo: Next.js and Vue.js are popular technologies for building modern websites, but they have different features and development approaches.
medium.conteudo_html:
Next.js and Vue.js are popular technologies for building modern websites, but they have different features and development approaches.

Next.js is a React-based framework that supports server-side rendering, static generation, and full-stack development. It is suitable for complex websites, e-commerce platforms, and applications that need flexible rendering options.

Vue.js is a JavaScript framework known for its simple syntax, flexibility, and beginner-friendly learning experience. It is useful for creating interactive interfaces and responsive websites.

Both technologies can deliver excellent performance when developed properly. Next.js is a good choice for developers working with React, while Vue.js is ideal for those who prefer a straightforward approach to frontend development.

Final Verdict: Choose Next.js for React-based applications and advanced framework features. Choose Vue.js for simplicity, flexibility, and an approachable learning experience.

medium.titulo: How Laravel and PHP Can Run in the Browser
medium.resumo: Write a component once in PHP. Run it on the server and in the browser, with the view you like.
medium.conteudo_html:
Write a component once in PHP. Run it on the server and in the browser, with the view you like.

What if your Laravel component, written once in PHP, could run in the browser too, and take a Vue, React, Solid or Svelte view as easily as a Blade one?

That question stayed with me for a long time. I’d built a client app with Inertia and Vue. It worked, but I kept writing things twice: validation in PHP and again in JavaScript, state on the server and again in the browser, plus an API in between just to move data around. I tried Fusion after that, and hit similar walls.

So in March 2025 I started working on the idea myself. It went through a few different repositories as I figured out what it should be. Eventually I moved everything into a project called Nitro, which, honestly, was on its way to becoming another abandoned side project of mine. Instead, it became the home for all of this.

I want to show you how it actually works, because the idea is simple once you see it.

A small component

Here’s a counter. It counts in the browser and saves on the server.


// app/Nitro/Components/Counter.php

namespace App\Nitro\Components;
use App\Models\Score;
use Nitro\Attributes\Server;
use Nitro\Component;

class Counter extends Component
{

  public int $count = 0;

  public function increment(): void
  {
    $this->count++;
  }

  #[Server]
  public function save(): void
  {
    Score::create(['value' => $this->count]);
  }

}

And its Blade view:

{{-- resources/views/nitro/components/counter.blade.php --}}

<div>
   <span>{{ $count }}</span>
   <button nitro:click="increment">+</button>
   <button nitro:click="save">Save</button>
</div>

You place it anywhere in Blade with:

<nitro:counter />

Nothing here is new to a Laravel or Livewire developer. A class, some public properties, two methods, a Blade view. The only unusual thing is #[Server] on one method. That one attribute is the line between “runs in the browser” and “runs on the server”.

One component, two languages

The trick is that Nitro keeps your component in two forms.

The first is your PHP class, exactly as you wrote it. Laravel runs it on the server, like any other code.

The second is the same class compiled to JavaScript. Nitro reads your PHP and writes the browser version for you. increment() becomes JavaScript that does what $this->count++ does. save() is left out, because it’s marked for the server, and the database has no business in the browser anyway.

PHP and JavaScript never call each other directly. They share the component, and they pass its state back and forth, the values of its public properties, signed by the server. Whichever side runs next starts from that state. That’s the whole handshake.

What happens, step by step

When you build with the command below, Nitro compiles each component’s PHP into JavaScript. It keeps PHP rules while it does this: arrays behave like PHP arrays, == compares the way PHP compares, string functions behave like PHP. And if you write a browser method that queries the database, the build fails and tells you the file and the line. You find out at your screen, not in production.

php artisan nitro:build

The first request. Laravel renders the page as it always does. The counter shows 0, the HTML is complete, search engines can read it. Along with the HTML, the page carries the counter’s state (count: 0), signed by the server.

The browser takes over. Nitro’s small runtime finds the counter in the page, creates it from the compiled JavaScript and fills it from the signed state. It does not render the page again, it just attaches to what’s there. Now the same counter is alive in the browser.

A click on +. The compiled increment() runs right there in the browser. count becomes 1, and only the part of the page that shows the count updates. This is your PHP, running as JavaScript.

A click on Save. save() is a server method, so Nitro sends the signed state to Laravel, with what changed (count: 1). The server checks the signature, rebuilds the real PHP Counter, runs save() with your database, mail and everything else Laravel has, and sends back the new signed state.

Why the browser can’t cheat

The obvious worry is, if the state lives in the browser, can’t someone change it?

They can try. The state is signed by the server and tied to the visitor’s session and user. If it’s changed, the server refuses it. On top of that, you have two attributes you’d expect:

  • #[Locked] on a property means the browser can’t change it at all. Use it for things like a post’s id.
  • #[Validate(‘required|max:120’)] checks a property’s value. Nitro shows the messages as the user types, and checks again on the server, which is the check that counts.

The rule I follow is simple. Anything that touches the database, sends mail or needs a secret goes in a #[Server] method. Everything else can run where the user is.

Now the part I care about most: any view you like

Blade is the default, and it’s great. But sometimes, the thing you need exists only for React, or your team already writes Vue, or a part of the page is mostly interaction and a JavaScript framework fits it better.

With Nitro, you keep the same PHP class and just change the view. One attribute does it:

// app/Nitro/Components/Counter.php

use Nitro\Attributes\View;

#[View(vue: 'counter')]
class Counter extends Component
{
 // the same class as before
}

Here’s the Vue view. No script tag, no imports:

<!-- resources/views/vue/counter.vue -->

<template>
  <div>
    <span>{{ count }}</span>
    <button @click="increment">+</button>
    <button @click="save" :disabled="save.processing">Save</button>
  </div>
</template>

And the same component with a React view (#[View(react: ‘counter’)] on the class):

// resources/views/react/counter.jsx

export default function Counter({ count, increment, save }) {
 return (
   <div>
     <span>{count}</span>
     <button onClick={increment}>+</button>
     <button onClick={save} disabled={save.processing}>Save</button>
   </div>
 );
}

How does the view get count and increment? Nitro hands the component to the framework in that framework’s own way. Each public property, each method and each computed value becomes a prop of its own, under its PHP name. A server method arrives as a function that makes the request, and it carries its status too, so save.processing tells you a save is running. Solid and Svelte get the same pieces as props. Vue gets them as names in the template. The view never sees the PHP object itself, and private things never reach it.

So the same class works with Blade, Vue, React, Solid and Svelte. You can even mix them on one page: a Vue list, a React chart and a Blade form side by side, talking to each other through events, none of them knowing what the others are written in.

I built a small blog five times to show this, once per framework, plus one page where all five work together. You can try them live in the docs:
https://nitrophp.com/docs/examples

What else it does

  • Pages and navigation: routed pages, and links that change the page without a full reload. Each page picks how a visit shows it: data (wait for its data, then show it complete), markup (show it at once, with placeholders until the data arrives) or client (render it in the browser, without asking the server).
  • Forms and validation: rules checked as you type, and again on the server.
  • File uploads, with progress and previews.
  • Events between components, and stores for state that several components share.
  • State in the address bar: a search or a filter kept in the URL.
  • Lazy and deferred loading: the slow parts of a page arrive after the rest.
  • Cached server results, and transitions when things appear and leave.
  • The page’s title and meta tags, for search engines and link previews.
  • Live updates from Laravel broadcasting (Reverb or Pusher).
  • Server rendering for Vue, React, Solid and Svelte views, if you want it.
  • Each JavaScript framework loads only on the pages that use it.
  • Tests for your components, written the way Laravel tests are.
  • Modules and packages: components in their own namespaces.

How it was built

I built Nitro with Claude Code as my pair programmer. I decided what Nitro should be and how it should work, and Claude Code helped write the design, test it and find the bugs I most certainly wouldd have missed on my own.

That’s also why testing matters so much in this project. Every change runs through a full test suite, including the same tests against the Blade, Vue, React, Solid and Svelte versions of a component, before anything is released.

When not to use it

I’d rather you hear this from me.

If your app is happy with Livewire, or your team is all-in on a separate JavaScript frontend with its own API, you probably don’t need Nitro. It’s also young. It’s tested heavily, but it doesn’t have years of production use behind it yet. There may be deeper bugs that only real apps will bring out. When they show up, I’ll fix them, the same way I’ve fixed the ones found so far. If you hit one, please open an issue on GitHub. It helps a lot.

Where it shines is when you want to stay in Laravel and PHP, and still reach for Vue, React, Solid or Svelte where they help, without building the glue yourself.

Try it

composer require nitro/nitro

  • Docs: https://nitrophp.com
  • How it works, in more detail: https://nitrophp.com/docs/how-it-works
  • GitHub: https://github.com/nitroframework/nitro

I’m building my own apps with Nitro, so it’ll keep getting work. If you try it, I’d love to hear what you think, good or bad.

Zeeshan Ali

corrida_no_ar.titulo: PARATLETA VENCE PROVA no geral e é DESCLASSIFICADO: entenda a regra
corrida_no_ar.resumo: A polêmica desclassificação de um paratleta que venceu no geral agita o mundo da corrida. E mais: o incrível calendário 2027 do Mountain Do, a nova e estilosa collab da Olympikus com Alexandre Herchcovitch, e os problemas que continuam na Meia das Três Fronteiras.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quarta-feira | 14 de outubro de 2026

O paratleta Júlio César Agripino, conhecido como Julião, venceu os 5 km da Track & Field Run Series no Shopping Iguatemi, com o tempo de 15 minutos e 24 segundos, mas foi desclassificado. O motivo, segundo ele, foi a presença de seu atleta-guia, que a organização considerou “ajuda externa”. A decisão gerou polêmica, mas está alinhada com as regras de arbitragem da Confederação Brasileira de Atletismo (CBAt). Para competir com um guia, o atleta deve se inscrever na categoria para pessoas com deficiência (PCD).

O problema é que, apesar de a prova oferecer a categoria PCD, não há premiação para os vencedores. Ou seja, mesmo que Julião competisse em sua categoria, não teria recebido prêmio algum. Em um depoimento, ele lamentou a situação e defendeu o direito de escolha dos atletas paralímpicos de competirem onde se sentirem mais à vontade. A desclassificação foi confirmada como correta por um árbitro da CBAt consultado pelo Corrida no Ar, mas o caso expõe a falta de incentivo e reconhecimento para atletas PCD em algumas provas.

Mountain Do divulga calendário para 2027

O circuito Mountain Do, conhecido por suas provas de trail run em locais espetaculares, já divulgou o calendário para 2027. O circuito contará com 10 etapas em 5 países, passando por diversos biomas como floresta, cerrado, montanha, ilha e deserto. Confira as datas e locais:

  • 14/03: Colônia de Sacramento, Uruguai
  • 03/04: Praia do Rosa, SC
  • 05/06: Deserto da Namíbia, Namíbia
  • 27/06: Chapada dos Veadeiros, GO
  • 10/07: Costão do Santinho, SC
  • 07/08: Fim do Mundo, Ushuaia (Argentina)
  • 11/09: Fernando de Noronha, PE
  • 26/09: Selva Amazônica, Macapá (AP)
  • 07/11: Deserto do Saara, Marrocos
  • 27/11: Pantanal, Rio Verde

Olympikus e Alexandre Herchcovitch lançam collab

A Olympikus anunciou uma colaboração com o estilista Alexandre Herchcovitch. A parceria resultou em edições limitadas e cheias de estilo dos modelos Corre 5 e Corre Trilha 3. Os tênis ganharam novas cores e padrões, com uma pegada que une performance e moda, saindo das pistas para as passarelas. A coleção já está disponível, mas com pares limitados.

Maratona de Maringá: Vagas dos 21k estão acabando

A Maratona de Maringá, que acontece nos dias 21 e 22 de novembro, já esgotou todas as vagas para a distância de 42 km. Para quem ainda deseja participar do evento, restam as últimas vagas para a prova de 21 km. Corra para garantir a sua inscrição antes que acabe!

Mais problemas na Meia das Três Fronteiras

A Meia Maratona das Três Fronteiras, que já foi alvo de críticas no ano passado, voltou a registrar problemas de organização. A principal reclamação desta edição foi o guarda-volumes. Corredores relataram que o serviço foi encerrado antes do horário previsto e que o caminhão responsável pelo transporte dos pertences partiu, deixando muitos atletas na mão. Alguns participantes, que haviam pago pelo serviço de transfer, precisaram correr com suas mochilas. Segundo os relatos, a situação foi caótica, com o caminhão quase atropelando corredores que tentavam deixar seus pertences.

Última etapa do ASICS Run Challenge

A etapa final do circuito ASICS Run Challenge acontecerá em Florianópolis, no dia 8 de novembro. O evento já passou por Belo Horizonte, Brasília, Fortaleza, Salvador e Recife, e agora se prepara para encerrar a temporada na capital catarinense. Se você planeja participar, pode usar o cupom CORRIDANOAR10 para garantir um desconto na sua inscrição.
